steps.label: The statement
lines: Photoelectric effect: when light of suitable
frequency falls on a metal surface, electrons
The ejected electrons are called photoelectrons.
steps.why: The effect is named for what happens, so the statement must contain light falling on a metal and electrons coming out. Naming the ejected electrons photoelectrons shows the term is understood.
common_mistakes: Writing that the metal glows or heats up. Electrons are ejected.
Leaving out the condition of suitable frequency, which is the whole point of the effect.
steps.memory_tip: Photo means light, electric means electrons. Light in, electrons out.
steps.margin_note: One sentence. The marks below are for the equation.

steps.label: Einstein's equation
lines: hν = energy of the incident photon
KE = kinetic energy of the electron = ½mv²

lines.text: hν = hν₀ + ½mv²   ⟹   KE = h(ν − ν₀)

steps.why: The photon's energy is spent in two ways: part of it frees the electron from the metal, and whatever is left becomes the electron's kinetic energy. Writing the equation as an energy balance is what makes the last line follow.
common_mistakes: Writing KE = hν and forgetting the work function.
Not saying what each symbol means. The terms carry marks here, not only the equation.
steps.memory_tip: Energy in equals energy to escape plus energy left over.
steps.margin_note: Both marks are here. Write the equation, then the meaning of every symbol.

steps.label: Threshold frequency and metals

lines.text: Below the threshold frequency ν₀ no electron is ejected

lines: This is true however intense the light is.
Alkali metals such as K, Rb and Cs show the
effect readily, because their work function
steps.why: Intensity sets how many photons arrive, not how much energy each one carries. One photon frees one electron, so if a single photon has less than the work function nothing is ejected no matter how many arrive.
common_mistakes: Saying bright enough light will always eject electrons. Frequency decides, not brightness.
Naming no metal at all. The alkali metals are the expected example.
steps.memory_tip: Brightness sends more photons. Frequency gives each photon more energy. Only the energy of each photon matters here.
steps.margin_note: Naming the threshold frequency and one alkali metal completes the answer.

insider_note: A three-star question that appears in almost every model paper. The energy balance hν = W₀ + KE with every symbol explained is where three of the four marks sit.
